title: Understand and Use Standard Deviation
description: Interpret standard deviation as spread, compare data sets conceptually, predict how changing values affects spread, and calculate standard deviation with Desmos.

blocks.html:
Standard deviation tells you about spread

Look for questions that use the term standard deviation. They may ask you to compare two data sets, predict what happens after a value changes, or calculate a standard deviation.

You do not need to calculate standard deviation by hand. You need to understand what it says and know how to ask Desmos for it.

Goal: Read standard deviation as a measure of spread from the center, predict whether it increases or decreases, and calculate it with stdev in Desmos.

Start by comparing the pictures

Both sets have mean \(10\). Set A stays close to \(10\), while Set B reaches much farther away.

Before you continue: decide which set has values that are typically farther from its mean.

figure.alt: Two dot plots with mean 10: Set A is clustered at 8 through 12, while Set B is spread from 2 through 18
figure.caption: Sets A and B.

content.prompt: Which set in the diagram should have the larger standard deviation?
choices: Set A, because its values are closer together
Set B, because its values are spread farther from the mean
The sets have equal standard deviations, because both means are \(10\)
There is not enough information unless every deviation is calculated
content.hint: Standard deviation is about spread. Compare how far the dots usually sit from the mean line.
content.explanation: Correct. Set B has the larger standard deviation because its values are typically farther from the mean.

blocks.html:
A non-technical meaning

Standard deviation describes a data set's typical distance from its mean. You can think of it as a spread meter.

  • Small standard deviation: values cluster near the mean.
  • Large standard deviation: values spread farther from the mean.

Standard deviation is never negative. A value of \(0\) means there is no spread at all.

Plain-English rule: more spread from the center means a larger standard deviation.

content.prompt: A data set has a very small standard deviation. What does that tell you?
choices: Its mean has to be small as well
It must contain very few values
Most values are close to the mean
Most values are negative
content.hint: Separate center from spread. Standard deviation describes how far values sit from the center.
content.explanation: Exactly. A small standard deviation means the values are tightly clustered around their mean.

blocks.html:
Mean and standard deviation answer different questions

  • Mean: Where is the center?
  • Standard deviation: How spread out are the values around that center?

Two sets can have the same mean and different standard deviations. Two sets can also have different means but the same standard deviation.

For example, \([1,2,3]\) and \([11,12,13]\) have the same shape and spread. The second set is simply shifted \(10\) units to the right.

content.prompt: Set P is \([4,5,6]\), and Set Q is \([14,15,16]\). How do their standard deviations compare?
choices: They are equal because the sets have the same spread
Set P's is larger because its values are smaller
Set Q's is larger because its mean is larger
They cannot be compared without combining the sets
content.hint: Every value in Set Q is exactly 10 more than the matching value in Set P. Did the distances among the values change?
content.explanation: Correct. The entire set shifted, but the spread stayed the same, so the standard deviations are equal.

blocks.html:
Compare standard deviations without calculating

  1. Find each set's center. A rough center is enough.
  2. Look at typical distances. Which set stays close to its own center?
  3. Notice extreme values. A value far from the rest usually increases spread.

Do not compare means and assume the larger mean has the larger standard deviation. Compare each set's spread around its own mean.

Decision: the set whose values are typically farther from its center has the larger standard deviation.

content.prompt: Which data set has the largest standard deviation?
content.hint: Ignore which set has the largest values. Compare how far each set spreads around its own center.
content.explanation: Right. \([2,6,10,14,18]\) reaches farthest from its center. The other three sets have the same narrow five-number pattern shifted to different centers.

blocks.html:
Adding one value: ask where it lands

When one new data value is added, compare it with the current center.

  • A new value near the center usually decreases the standard deviation.
  • A new value far from the center usually increases the standard deviation.

The mean may move a little, but distance from the main cluster is still the key idea.

Prediction question: Does the new value join the cluster or stretch the set outward?

content.prompt: The data set is \([8,9,10,11,12]\). Which added value would most likely increase its standard deviation?
content.hint: The current set clusters around 10. Which choice would stretch the set farthest away?
content.explanation: Correct. Adding \(30\) creates a value far from the cluster, so the spread and standard deviation increase.

blocks.html:
Removing one value reverses the question

  • Removing a value far from the center usually decreases the standard deviation.
  • Removing a value near the center can increase the standard deviation because the remaining values are less concentrated.

Focus on what remains. If the removal makes the set tighter, standard deviation decreases. If it leaves mostly farther-apart values, standard deviation increases.

content.prompt: The data set is \([4,5,5,5,6,20]\). Which change will most clearly decrease its standard deviation?
choices: Remove one \(5\)
Remove \(4\)
Remove \(6\)
Remove \(20\)
content.hint: Which value is farthest from the main cluster near 5?
content.explanation: Exactly. Removing \(20\) removes the farthest value and makes the remaining set much tighter.

blocks.html:
Replacing a value: track its movement

A replacement removes one value and adds another. Compare the old and new positions.

  • Move a value toward the center and standard deviation usually decreases.
  • Move a value away from the center and standard deviation usually increases.

You usually do not need exact arithmetic. Decide whether the replacement tightens or stretches the set.

content.prompt: The data set is \([3,4,5,6,20]\). What happens to its standard deviation if \(20\) is replaced by \(7\)?
choices: It decreases because the replacement moves toward the cluster
It increases, because \(7\) is greater than \(6\)
It stays the same because the number of values is unchanged
It drops to zero, because the outlier disappears
content.hint: Compare how far 20 and 7 sit from the main cluster near 5.
content.explanation: Correct. Replacing \(20\) with \(7\) pulls the extreme value toward the center, so the set becomes less spread out.

blocks.html:
Do not confuse adding a value with adding to every value

Adding one new value can change spread. Adding the same amount to every value only shifts the whole set.

For example:

\[[2,4,6]\longrightarrow[12,14,16]\]

Every value increased by \(10\), but the gaps and distances from the mean stayed the same.

Shift rule: adding or subtracting the same constant from every value does not change standard deviation.

content.prompt: Every value in a data set is decreased by \(7\). What happens to the standard deviation?
choices: It decreases by \(7\)
It increases by \(7\)
It stays the same
It becomes negative
content.hint: The center shifts by 7 too. Think about whether any distance from the center changes.
content.explanation: Right. The entire set shifts together, so its spread and standard deviation stay the same.

blocks.html:
Zero means every value is identical

If all values equal the mean, every distance from the mean is zero. Therefore the standard deviation is zero.

For example, \([7,7,7,7]\) has standard deviation \(0\).

If even one value differs, the set has some spread and its standard deviation is greater than zero.

content.prompt: Which data set has standard deviation \(0\)?
content.hint: Zero spread means no value is different from any other value.
content.explanation: Correct. Every value in \([6,6,6,6]\) is identical, so every distance from the mean is zero.

blocks.html:
Calculate standard deviation directly in Desmos

The stdev function finds standard deviation. In the embedded SAT calculator, you can type the data values directly:

\[\operatorname{stdev}(2,3,4,5,6)\]

Use commas between values and close the parenthesis. Desmos displays approximately \(1.58\).

Try it: Type stdev(2,3,4,5,6) in the open calculator and read the result.

content.prompt: What does Desmos return for \(\operatorname{stdev}(2,3,4,5,6)\)?
choices: Approximately \(0.71\)
Exactly \(2\)
Approximately \(1.58\)
Exactly \(4\)
content.hint: Read the decimal displayed below the stdev expression.
content.explanation: Correct. Desmos reports approximately \(1.58\). You can use the displayed decimal; you do not need the hand-calculation formula.

blocks.html:
A named list is better when data may change

On the first line, assign the list to a variable:

\[A=[2,3,4,5,6]\]

On the second line, enter:

\[\operatorname{stdev}(A)\]

This gives the same result as direct entry. The advantage is that you can edit \(A\) once and every expression using \(A\) updates automatically.

Preferred workflow: define the list, then apply stdev to its name.

content.prompt: Why is \(A=[2,3,4,5,6]\) followed by \(\operatorname{stdev}(A)\) often better than direct entry?
choices: You can edit the list once and every calculation using \(A\) updates
A named list always makes the standard deviation smaller
Desmos cannot calculate a standard deviation from direct values
The letter \(A\) changes the data into an equation
content.hint: Think about comparing an original set with a changed version or correcting one mistyped value.
content.explanation: Exactly. A named list keeps the data reusable, so editing the list updates \(\operatorname{stdev}(A)\) automatically.

blocks.html:
Use named lists to compare two sets

The calculator shows:

\[A=[8,9,10,11,12]\]

\[B=[2,6,10,14,18]\]

and calculates both standard deviations. The lists have the same mean, but \(B\) is much more spread out.

Connect the ideas: your visual prediction and the Desmos values should agree.

content.prompt: What do the Desmos results confirm about Sets A and B?
choices: Set A has the larger standard deviation because its values are consecutive
The standard deviations are equal because the means are equal
Set B has the smaller standard deviation because it includes 10
Set B has the larger standard deviation because it is more spread out
content.hint: Compare the two displayed stdev values and connect the larger value with the more spread-out list.
content.explanation: Correct. Desmos confirms the conceptual comparison: Set B is more spread out, so its standard deviation is larger.

blocks.html:
Predict first, then check a changed value

Set \(C\) is \([8,9,10,11,12]\). Set \(D\) replaces \(12\) with \(20\).

Before reading the outputs, predict which set has the larger standard deviation. Then compare \(\operatorname{stdev}(C)\) and \(\operatorname{stdev}(D)\).

Use Desmos as a check: the value farther from the cluster should stretch the spread.

content.prompt: Why is \(\operatorname{stdev}(D)\) larger than \(\operatorname{stdev}(C)\)?
choices: Set D's values produce a larger mean than set C's values do
Replacing \(12\) with \(20\) moves one value farther from the cluster
Set D uses a different list letter in the calculator
Each replacement increases a set's standard deviation
content.hint: Compare the positions of the old value 12 and the new value 20 relative to the other four values.
content.explanation: Right. The replacement stretches the set outward. The reason is distance from the cluster, not the list name or the fact that a replacement occurred.

blocks.html:
A four-step process for standard-deviation questions

  1. Identify the task. Compare, predict a change, or calculate.
  2. Find the center and spread. Look for clustering and far values.
  3. Track the change. Does it tighten the set, stretch it, or shift every value together?
  4. Use Desmos when a number is required. Enter stdev(values), or define a named list and enter stdev(list name).

Do not calculate by hand unless explicitly required: reason about spread first, then use Desmos for the value.

content.prompt: A question replaces one data value and asks whether standard deviation increases or decreases. What should you examine first?
choices: Whether the newly inserted value is positive or negative
Whether the total number of values stayed the same
Whether the replacement moved toward or away from the set's center
Whether the set's mean works out to a whole number
content.hint: Standard deviation measures spread from the center.
content.explanation: Correct. Track the replacement's distance from the center: toward the center usually decreases spread; away usually increases it.

content.prompt: The data set is \([0,10]\). The value \(5\), which is the mean, is added. What happens to the standard deviation?
choices: It decreases because the new value joins the center of the set
It increases because the set has more values
It stays the same because the old endpoints did not move
It becomes zero because the mean was added
content.solution:
The set \([0,10]\) has mean \(5\), and both values sit \(5\) away from that center.
Adding the value \(5\) places a new data point exactly at the mean, so ask the prediction question: does it join the cluster or stretch the set outward?
It joins the center: the set becomes \([0,5,10]\), the endpoints stay put, and a larger share of the data now sits at zero distance from the mean.
More concentration near the center means a smaller typical distance from the mean, so the standard deviation decreases.
So the answer is choice A, it decreases because the new value joins the center of the set.
content.hint: Ask whether adding 5 makes the values more concentrated around the center.
content.explanation: Correct. Adding a value at the mean increases the concentration near the center, so the standard deviation decreases.

content.prompt: The data set is \([0,5,10]\). The center value \(5\) is removed. What happens to the standard deviation?
choices: It decreases because there are fewer values
It becomes zero because only two values remain
It stays the same because 0 and 10 did not change
It increases because only the two far-apart endpoints remain
content.solution:
The set \([0,5,10]\) has mean \(5\): the value \(5\) sits at the center, while \(0\) and \(10\) sit at the edges.
Removing \(5\) takes away the only value at zero distance from the mean, leaving \([0,10]\).
Every remaining value is now a full \(5\) from the mean, so the typical distance from the center goes up even though the endpoints never moved.
Less concentration near the center means a larger standard deviation.
So the answer is choice D, it increases because only the two far-apart endpoints remain.
content.hint: Compare the concentration of [0,5,10] with the remaining set [0,10].
content.explanation: Right. Removing the central value leaves only the far-apart endpoints, so the remaining set is more spread out.

content.prompt: Use Desmos to find \(\operatorname{stdev}(1,2,3)\). What is the result?
content.solution:
In Desmos, type \(\operatorname{stdev}(1,2,3)\) exactly, with commas between the values.
Desmos handles the computation and returns \(1\).
The result is reasonable: the mean of the set is \(2\), and every value sits within \(1\) of that center, so a spread of \(1\) fits the data.
So the answer is choice B, \(1\).
content.hint: Type stdev(1,2,3) exactly, using commas between the values.
content.explanation: Correct. Desmos returns \(1\). The calculator handles the computation; your job is to enter the data accurately and interpret the result.

content.prompt: Order the data sets from smallest standard deviation to largest standard deviation: P = \([5,5,5,5]\), Q = \([4,5,5,6]\), R = \([0,5,5,10]\).
choices: R, Q, P
Q, P, R
P, Q, R
P, R, Q
content.hint: P has no spread. Q stays close to 5. R reaches farthest from 5.
content.explanation: Exactly. P has standard deviation 0, Q has a small spread around 5, and R has the largest spread.

content.prompt: Data set A consists of the values \(42, 44, 45, 47\), and data set B consists of the values \(30, 40, 50, 60\). Which statement correctly compares the standard deviations of the two data sets?
choices: The standard deviation of data set A is less than the standard deviation of data set B.
The standard deviation of data set A is greater than the standard deviation of data set B.
The standard deviations are equal because both data sets contain four values.
The standard deviations cannot be compared without knowing each data set's median.
content.hint: Reason about spread from each mean before calculating anything.
content.explanation: Correct. Set A's values cluster within a few units of their mean, while set B's sit \(10\) or more away, so B has the larger spread. Equal counts do not make spreads equal, and Desmos stdev confirms: about \(2.1\) versus \(12.9\).

content.prompt: Without looking back, which summary is correct?
choices: Standard deviation measures spread from the mean; farther values decrease spread, and Desmos stdev can calculate it
Standard deviation measures spread from the median; values above the mean increase spread, and Desmos total can calculate it
Standard deviation measures the gap between the largest and smallest values; adding any value increases it, and Desmos mean calculates it
Standard deviation measures spread from the mean; farther values increase spread, and Desmos stdev can calculate it
content.hint: Recall the plain-English meaning and the Desmos function name.
content.explanation: You have it. Standard deviation describes spread around the mean. Reason about whether values move toward or away from the center, and use stdev in Desmos when you need the numerical value.

content.html:
You can interpret and calculate standard deviation

You can compare spread without a formula, predict how changing values affects the spread, distinguish a new value from a whole-set shift, and use direct or named-list stdev entries in Desmos.
